name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: The company given to the planet
items.fact: In 2022, Patagonia's founder Yvon Chouinard gave the outdoor-clothing company away to a trust and a charity that fight climate change. He said: “Earth is now our only shareholder.”

items.name: The pharmacy without cigarettes
items.fact: In 2014, CVS, one of America's biggest pharmacy chains, stopped selling cigarettes in all its shops, even though they brought in about $2 billion a year.

items.name: The banned Christmas advert
items.fact: In 2018, the UK supermarket Iceland used a Greenpeace cartoon about an orangutan losing its forest to palm-oil farms as its Christmas advert. It was blocked from British TV for being too political.

items.name: Lego drops Shell
items.fact: In 2014, after a Greenpeace video showing a Lego Arctic drowning in oil went viral, Lego decided to end its 50-year marketing deal with the oil company Shell.

items.name: The free seatbelt
items.fact: In 1959, Volvo patented the three-point seatbelt, invented by its engineer Nils Bohlin. Instead of keeping it for itself, Volvo let every other car maker use the design for free.

items.name: The pay cap
items.fact: At the American soap company Dr. Bronner's, the best-paid bosses may earn no more than five times what the lowest-paid full-time worker gets.

items.name: Shares for everyone
items.fact: In 2016, Hamdi Ulukaya, the founder of the American yoghurt maker Chobani, gave his 2,000 full-time workers shares that could add up to 10 per cent of the company.

items.name: The unfair chocolate bar
items.fact: The Dutch chocolate brand Tony's Chocolonely divides its bars into pieces of different sizes. The unequal pieces are meant to remind you how unequally money is shared in the cocoa industry.

items.name: The toilet sit-in
items.fact: The Australian toilet-paper brand Who Gives A Crap gives half its profits to build toilets. To start it, a founder sat on a toilet for 50 hours, filmed live, until enough money was raised.

items.name: Closed on Black Friday
items.fact: In 2015, the American outdoor shop REI closed all its stores on Black Friday, one of the biggest shopping days of the year, and paid its 12,000 staff to spend the day outside.

fakes.name: The farmer's phone number
fakes.fact: A German supermarket chain prints a photo of the farmer, and their phone number, on every bag of potatoes. Farmers get about five calls a week, mostly to ask for recipes.

fakes.name: The pay-gap loan rule
fakes.fact: A Dutch bank refuses to lend money to any company whose boss earns more than 20 times the average worker there. It says it has turned down 140 companies since 2019.

fakes.name: The keep-your-phone refund
fakes.fact: A Finnish phone-case maker gives customers 5 euros back for every year they keep the same phone. To claim it, they send a photo of the phone with that day's newspaper.

fakes.name: The drought price
fakes.fact: An Australian brewery raises the price of its beer by 20 cents in dry years and gives the extra money to farmers hit by drought. Sales have gone up in every drought year so far.

fakes.name: The wage on the packet
fakes.fact: An Italian pasta maker prints the hourly wage of its wheat farmers on every packet. When a supermarket asked it to remove the number, it moved the pasta to another supermarket.

fakes.name: The trainer for the maker
fakes.fact: For every 100 pairs it sells, a Spanish trainer brand gives a free pair to a worker in the factory that made them. The workers choose the colour, and one colour became a best-seller.

fakes.name: The hedgehog advertising budget
fakes.fact: A Danish crisp brand gives half its advertising budget to a hedgehog rescue charity. Its only advert now is a hedgehog on the back of every bag, and sales have doubled.

fakes.name: The train-pass company cars
fakes.fact: A Norwegian energy company replaced all 300 of its company cars with first-class train passes for staff. Twelve managers left, but the company says it saved money in the first year.

fakes.name: The tax label
fakes.fact: A Dutch clothing brand sews a second label into every item showing how much tax the company paid on it. A T-shirt costing 30 euros carries a label saying “Tax paid: 2.40 euros”.

fakes.name: The fountain supermarket
fakes.fact: A Portuguese supermarket chain stopped selling bottled water and put free drinking fountains in all its shops instead. It lost money on water but says customers stay longer.

tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small problem (“most of the calls are about recipes”): perfect ideas sound fake.
